_about: Short biographies for the writer pages that rebuild-author-catalogue.js generates. Each entry: the section heading and one or more paragraphs of trusted HTML (titles in <i>). Check every date and name against a reliable source before changing one.

Henry James.heading: Henry James’s life.
paragraphs: Henry James was born in New York in 1843 and spent much of his childhood moving between America and Europe with his family. He settled in London in 1876, made his name with Daisy Miller (1878) and The Portrait of a Lady (1881), and wrote for the rest of his life about Americans and Europeans misreading one another. He became a British subject in 1915 and died in London the following year.

The Turn of the Screw ran as a serial in Collier’s Weekly in 1898 and came out as a book later that year. In 1934 Edmund Wilson argued that the ghosts are the governess’s delusions. The story itself never settles whether she sees them or imagines them.

Henrik Ibsen.heading: Ibsen’s life.
paragraphs: Henrik Ibsen was born in Skien, Norway, in 1828. His father’s business failed when he was a boy, and at fifteen he was apprenticed to a pharmacist in Grimstad. He learned the theatre as a writer and director in Bergen and Christiania, then left Norway in 1864 and lived in Italy and Germany for twenty-seven years. There he wrote Brand, Peer Gynt and the prose plays of modern life that made him famous across Europe. He returned to Norway in 1891 and died in Christiania in 1906.

A Doll’s House was published in December 1879 and first staged in Copenhagen that month. For the German premiere the leading actress refused to play a mother who leaves her children, and Ibsen, to prevent a worse version by someone else, wrote an alternative ending in which Nora stays. He called it a barbaric outrage on the play.

L. M. Montgomery.heading: Montgomery’s life.
paragraphs: Lucy Maud Montgomery was born in Prince Edward Island in 1874. Her mother died before she was two, and she was brought up by her grandparents in Cavendish, the farming village that became Avonlea. She trained as a teacher, worked for a year on a Halifax newspaper and wrote in the evenings. Anne of Green Gables was turned down by several publishers and put away in a hatbox before L. C. Page of Boston took it; it came out in 1908 and was an immediate success.

In 1911 she married a Presbyterian minister, Ewan Macdonald, and spent the rest of her life in Ontario, where she wrote seven more Anne books among many others. The Blue Castle (1926), one of her few novels for adults, is set in the Muskoka lake country of Ontario. She died in Toronto in 1942.

William Hope Hodgson.heading: Hodgson’s life.
paragraphs: William Hope Hodgson was born in Essex in 1877, the son of a clergyman, and went to sea as a cabin boy at thirteen. In eight years as an apprentice and seaman he won a Royal Humane Society medal for rescuing a man who had fallen overboard. He came ashore to run a school of physical culture in Blackburn, where in 1902 he challenged Houdini to escape from his handcuffs.

The sea is in most of what he wrote, from The Boats of the “Glen Carrig” (1907) to The Ghost Pirates (1909). The House on the Borderland appeared in 1908, and the Carnacki stories, about a detective who investigates hauntings, were collected in 1913. Hodgson joined the army in the First World War and was killed by a shell near Ypres in April 1918.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge.heading: Coleridge’s life.
paragraphs: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was born in 1772 at Ottery St Mary in Devon, the youngest son of the vicar. He went to Christ’s Hospital and to Cambridge, which he left without a degree after a few months as a trooper in the dragoons under an assumed name. He planned with Robert Southey to found an ideal community in America, married Sara Fricker, and settled at Nether Stowey in Somerset, where William and Dorothy Wordsworth came to live nearby in 1797. Lyrical Ballads (1798) came out of that friendship and opens with his Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

“Kubla Khan” and “Christabel” belong to the same years, though neither was printed until 1816. Opium and illness broke up his marriage and much of his work, but he went on lecturing and writing criticism, including the Biographia Literaria (1817). From 1816 he lived with the surgeon James Gillman at Highgate, where he died in 1834.

William Wordsworth.heading: Wordsworth’s life.
paragraphs: William Wordsworth was born in 1770 at Cockermouth on the edge of the Lake District and lost both parents before he was fourteen. After Cambridge he spent a year in revolutionary France, where he fell in love with Annette Vallon, who bore him a daughter. Back in England he lived with his sister Dorothy, and in 1797 they moved to Alfoxden in Somerset to be near Coleridge. Lyrical Ballads (1798) came out of that friendship, and Wordsworth added his Preface to the second edition of 1800.

From 1799 he lived in Grasmere, at Dove Cottage and later at Rydal Mount nearby, and in 1802 he married Mary Hutchinson. He became Poet Laureate in 1843 and died in 1850. The Prelude, the long poem about his own growth that he revised for half a century, was published a few months after his death.

M. R. James.heading: M. R. James’s life.
paragraphs: Montague Rhodes James was born in Kent in 1862 and grew up at Great Livermere in Suffolk, where his father was rector. He spent almost his whole life at Eton and at King’s College, Cambridge: he was a student, then a fellow, Director of the Fitzwilliam Museum, Provost of King’s and finally Provost of Eton, where he died in 1936. His scholarly work was on medieval manuscripts, and he catalogued the manuscripts of nearly every Cambridge college.

The ghost stories began as entertainments read aloud to friends at Christmas. Ghost Stories of an Antiquary appeared in 1904, three more volumes followed, and the collected stories were published in 1931. Many of his ghosts come out of the things he knew best: old books, church furnishings and college archives.

Edgar Allan Poe.heading: Poe’s life.
paragraphs: Edgar Allan Poe was born in Boston in 1809 to two actors, and was an orphan before he was three. John Allan, a Richmond merchant, took him in but never adopted him, and the two quarrelled over money for years. Poe left the University of Virginia in debt, served in the army and was dismissed from West Point, then made a precarious living as a magazine editor and critic in Richmond, Philadelphia and New York.

He wrote his tales for magazines, from “The Fall of the House of Usher” (1839) to “The Tell-Tale Heart” (1843), and with “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” (1841) he wrote the first modern detective story. “The Raven” (1845) made him famous but not prosperous. His wife, Virginia, died in 1847, and he died in Baltimore in 1849, in circumstances that have never been explained.

T. E. Lawrence.heading: Lawrence’s life.
paragraphs: Thomas Edward Lawrence was born in North Wales in 1888 and grew up in Oxford. He read history at Jesus College, wrote his thesis on Crusader castles after walking more than a thousand miles through Syria, and worked before the war as an archaeologist at Carchemish on the Euphrates. In 1916 British intelligence in Cairo sent him to the Arab Revolt, and he served with Emir Faisal’s forces until the capture of Damascus in 1918.

He began Seven Pillars of Wisdom in 1919, lost most of the first draft at Reading station that year and wrote it again. A subscribers’ edition was printed privately in 1926, and the book went on general sale only in 1935, two months after Lawrence died following a motorcycle accident in Dorset. In the years between he had enlisted in the ranks of the RAF and the Tank Corps under the names Ross and Shaw.

Kate Chopin.heading: Chopin’s life.
paragraphs: Kate Chopin was born Katherine O’Flaherty in St Louis in 1850. At twenty she married Oscar Chopin, a cotton factor, and lived in New Orleans and then in rural Natchitoches Parish, raising six children. Oscar died in 1882, and two years later she went home to St Louis, where she began to write at the end of her thirties.

Her stories of Creole and Cajun Louisiana, collected in Bayou Folk (1894) and A Night in Acadie (1897), made her reputation. The Awakening (1899) damaged it: reviewers condemned Edna Pontellier’s desires, and Chopin published little afterwards. She died in 1904, and the novel was largely forgotten until scholars took it up again in the 1950s and 1960s.

George Grossmith.heading: George Grossmith’s life.
paragraphs: George Grossmith was born in London in 1847, the son of a journalist and lecturer. He followed his father as a reporter at Bow Street police court before making his name as a comic entertainer at the piano. In 1877 he was cast in Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Sorcerer, and for the next twelve years he created the leading comic parts in their operas, among them Sir Joseph Porter, the Major-General, Bunthorne, the Lord Chancellor and Ko-Ko.

He wrote The Diary of a Nobody with his brother Weedon. It ran in Punch in 1888 and 1889 and came out as a book, enlarged and illustrated by Weedon, in 1892. George went back to touring as a solo entertainer and died in Folkestone in 1912.

Weedon Grossmith.heading: Weedon Grossmith’s life.
paragraphs: Weedon Grossmith was born in London in 1854, seven years after his brother George. He trained as a painter at the Slade and the Royal Academy Schools and exhibited at the Academy, but in the 1880s he went on the stage and became a popular comic actor, often of nervous, put-upon little men not unlike Mr Pooter. He later managed the Vaudeville Theatre and wrote plays of his own.

The Diary of a Nobody was a joint book. The brothers wrote it together for Punch, and Weedon drew the illustrations for the book edition of 1892. His memoir, From Studio to Stage, came out in 1913, and he died in 1919.

Jack London.heading: Jack London’s life.
paragraphs: Jack London was born in San Francisco in 1876 and grew up poor across the bay in Oakland. Before he was twenty-one he had worked in a cannery, raided oyster beds, sailed on a sealing schooner to Japan and tramped across America. In 1897 he joined the Klondike gold rush, came home the next year with scurvy and no gold, and started writing about the North.

The Call of the Wild (1903) made him famous, and White Fang (1906) told the same story in reverse: a wolf dog that comes in from the wild to live with people. London became one of the best-paid writers in America, a lecturer for socialism and the owner of a large ranch in Sonoma County, where he died in 1916, aged forty.

Wilkie Collins.heading: Collins’s life.
paragraphs: Wilkie Collins was born in London in 1824, the son of the landscape painter William Collins, who named him after his friend the painter Sir David Wilkie. He worked for a tea merchant and trained as a barrister without ever practising. In 1851 he met Charles Dickens, who became his closest friend and published much of his work in his magazines Household Words and All the Year Round.

The Woman in White ran in All the Year Round in 1859 and 1860, and The Moonstone followed in the same magazine in 1868. Collins took laudanum for gout for most of his adult life and kept two households, one with Caroline Graves and one with Martha Rudd, the mother of his three children. He died in London in 1889.

Stephen Crane.heading: Crane’s life.
paragraphs: Stephen Crane was born in Newark, New Jersey, in 1871, the fourteenth child of a Methodist minister. He left college after a year and worked as a reporter in New York, where he paid to print his first novel, Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893). The Red Badge of Courage made him famous in 1895; he wrote it before he had seen a battle, from talk with veterans and illustrated histories of the Civil War.

He then reported on wars in Greece and Cuba. On the way to Cuba in January 1897 his ship, the Commodore, sank off Florida and he spent about thirty hours in a small boat, the experience behind “The Open Boat”. He settled in England with Cora Taylor and died of tuberculosis in Germany in 1900, at twenty-eight.

E. Nesbit.heading: Nesbit’s life.
paragraphs: Edith Nesbit was born in London in 1858; her father, an agricultural chemist, died when she was three. In 1880 she married Hubert Bland, and in 1884 they were among the founders of the Fabian Society. Bland earned little, and Nesbit kept the household, which came to include his two children by another woman, with journalism, verse and stories.

Her books for children, beginning with The Story of the Treasure Seekers (1899), changed the form: her children are funny, quarrelsome and real. The Railway Children ran as a serial in 1905 and came out as a book in 1906. She also wrote ghost and horror stories for adults, collected in Grim Tales (1893) and Fear (1910). She died in Kent in 1924.

Algernon Blackwood.heading: Blackwood’s life.
paragraphs: Algernon Blackwood was born in Kent in 1869 into a strict evangelical family, and was educated at Wellington College and at a Moravian school in the Black Forest. In his twenties he went to Canada and then to New York, where he tried farming and business before working as a newspaper reporter, and he spent his holidays in the forests of Ontario and Quebec. He came back to England in 1899 and began publishing ghost stories in his late thirties.

“The Willows” (1907) came out of a canoe trip down the Danube, and “The Wendigo” (1910) out of hunting trips in the Canadian woods. He belonged for a time to the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, and late in life he became well known on BBC radio and television as a teller of ghost stories. He died in 1951.

Jerome K. Jerome.heading: Jerome’s life.
paragraphs: Jerome Klapka Jerome was born in Walsall in 1859 and grew up in East London, where his father’s business failures kept the family poor. He left school at fourteen to work as a railway clerk at Euston, and tried acting, teaching and journalism before his first books, sketches of stage life and the humorous essays of Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow (1886), began to sell.

Three Men in a Boat (1889) was written soon after his marriage, from boating trips with his friends George Wingrave and Carl Hentschel, and began as a guide to the Thames with comic interludes. It sold in enormous numbers. Jerome edited The Idler with Robert Barr, wrote plays, drove an ambulance for the French army in the First World War, and died in 1927.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.heading: Dostoevsky’s life.
paragraphs: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born in Moscow in 1821, the son of a doctor at a hospital for the poor. He trained as a military engineer in St Petersburg, resigned to write, and was famous at twenty-four with his first novel, Poor Folk (1846). White Nights followed in 1848. The next year he was arrested for belonging to a socialist discussion circle, sentenced to death and led out to be shot before a reprieve was read. He served four years of hard labour in Siberia and five more as a soldier.

Back in St Petersburg he wrote Notes from Underground (1864) and then, often in debt and struggling with epilepsy and gambling, the great novels: Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov, which appeared in 1879 and 1880. He died in St Petersburg in 1881, a few months after finishing it.

Sheridan Le Fanu.heading: Le Fanu’s life.
paragraphs: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu was born in Dublin in 1814 into a family of Huguenot descent; the playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan was his great-uncle. He studied law at Trinity College, Dublin, and was called to the bar, but went into journalism instead, and from 1861 he owned and edited the Dublin University Magazine. After his wife died in 1858 he withdrew almost entirely from society.

His best-known novel, Uncle Silas, appeared in 1864. Carmilla was serialised in the magazine The Dark Blue in 1871 and 1872 and collected in 1872 in In a Glass Darkly, framed, like the other stories there, as a case from the papers of the physician Dr Hesselius. Le Fanu died in Dublin in 1873.

Thomas Paine.heading: Paine’s life.
paragraphs: Thomas Paine was born in Thetford, Norfolk, in 1737, the son of a Quaker staymaker. He followed his father’s trade, then became an excise officer and was dismissed twice. In London in 1774 he met Benjamin Franklin, who gave him letters of introduction, and he sailed for Philadelphia. Common Sense, published in January 1776, argued plainly for independence and sold in enormous numbers; the first number of The American Crisis followed that December, and Washington had it read to his troops.

After the war Paine went back to Europe. Rights of Man (1791–92), his defence of the French Revolution, led to his trial in England for seditious libel; by then he was in France, where he was elected to the National Convention and later imprisoned for ten months. He returned to America in 1802 and died in New York in 1809.

Leo Tolstoy.heading: Tolstoy’s life.
paragraphs: Leo Tolstoy was born in 1828 on his family’s estate at Yasnaya Polyana, south of Moscow, and lost both parents before he was ten. He left Kazan University without a degree, served as an artillery officer in the Caucasus and at the siege of Sevastopol, and wrote about both. In 1862 he married Sophia Behrs, who bore him thirteen children and copied out his manuscripts, and over the next fifteen years he wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

At about fifty he went through a religious crisis, described in A Confession, and afterwards wrote mainly moral and religious works and shorter fiction. The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) was the first major story of this period. He was excommunicated by the Orthodox Church in 1901, and in 1910, at eighty-two, he left home secretly and died of pneumonia at the railway station at Astapovo.

E. F. Benson.heading: Benson’s life.
paragraphs: Edward Frederic Benson was born in 1867 at Wellington College, where his father was headmaster; his father later became Archbishop of Canterbury, and his brothers A. C. and R. H. Benson were writers too. After Marlborough and King’s College, Cambridge, he worked for some years at the British School at Athens, and his first novel, Dodo (1893), a society comedy, was a best-seller.

He wrote nearly a hundred books and is best known now for the Mapp and Lucia comedies and for his ghost stories, which appeared in collections from The Room in the Tower (1912) to More Spook Stories (1934). He lived for many years at Lamb House in Rye, which had been Henry James’s house, served three terms as the town’s mayor, and died in 1940.

Joseph Conrad.heading: Conrad’s life.
paragraphs: Joseph Conrad was born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski in 1857, to Polish parents in a part of Ukraine then ruled by Russia. His father, a poet and translator, was exiled for nationalist conspiracy, and Conrad was an orphan by eleven. At sixteen he went to Marseilles and to sea, joined the British merchant navy in 1878, and in 1886 qualified as a master and became a British subject. English was his third language, after Polish and French.

In 1890 he went to the Congo Free State and took a river steamer up the Congo to Stanley Falls; the journey lies behind Heart of Darkness, serialised in Blackwood’s Magazine in 1899. His first novel, Almayer’s Folly, appeared in 1895, after he had left the sea, and Lord Jim, Nostromo and The Secret Agent followed. He died in Kent in 1924.

Alexander Pope.heading: Pope’s life.
paragraphs: Alexander Pope was born in London in 1688, the son of a Catholic linen merchant. As a Catholic he could not go to university, vote or hold office, and the family moved out to Binfield in Windsor Forest, where he largely taught himself. A tubercular infection of the spine in childhood stunted his growth, and he was in pain and poor health all his life.

An Essay on Criticism (1711) made his name at twenty-three. The Rape of the Lock appeared in two cantos in 1712 and in the five-canto version, with its sylphs, in 1714. His translations of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey made him rich enough to live independently, at a villa at Twickenham with a famous grotto, and he spent his later years on satire and philosophical verse, from The Dunciad to An Essay on Man. He died at Twickenham in 1744.

Nikolai Gogol.heading: Gogol’s life.
paragraphs: Nikolai Gogol was born in 1809 in the Poltava region of Ukraine, into a family of minor Cossack gentry. At nineteen he went to St Petersburg, failed as a clerk and as an actor, and bought up and burned the copies of his first published poem when reviewers mocked it. Then Evenings on a Farm near Dikanka (1831–32), comic and supernatural tales of Ukrainian village life, made him famous.

His St Petersburg stories, from “Nevsky Prospect” and “Diary of a Madman” to “The Overcoat” (1842), and his play The Government Inspector (1836) are full of petty officials, some comic and some frightening. He lived mostly in Rome while he wrote the first part of Dead Souls (1842). In his last years religious anxiety took over, and shortly before he died in Moscow in 1852 he burned the manuscript of its second part.

William Blake.heading: Blake’s life.
paragraphs: William Blake was born in London in 1757, the son of a hosier, and had almost no schooling outside a drawing school. At fourteen he was apprenticed to the engraver James Basire, and he earned his living as an engraver for the rest of his life. In 1782 he married Catherine Boucher, who signed the register with a cross; he taught her to read, and she worked beside him at the press.

In the late 1780s he invented a way of etching words and pictures together on one copper plate. Songs of Innocence appeared in 1789 and the combined Songs of Innocence and of Experience in 1794, each copy printed by the Blakes and coloured by hand, so that no two are quite alike. He sold few, and when he died in 1827 he was known mainly as an eccentric engraver.
